Empirical Research Plan  

======================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two–Stage Least Squares (2SLS) / Instrumental‐Variables hedonic price estimation, followed by an inverse-demand step to derive welfare measures for different income groups.

Why IV is appropriate  

•  The question is contemporaneous (one 1984 cross-section); DID or event-study designs require panel/time variation that is absent.  
•  Spatial Regression Discontinuity (green-belt border) is attractive for a single headline estimate, but IV is preferable because we need *multiple* planning-generated amenities (accessible open space, inaccessible open space, industrial land) simultaneously and wish to translate them into household-level WTP curves.  
•  Planning designations set decades earlier are plausibly exogenous to 1984 household sorting yet are strong predictors of current land-use shares – exactly the classic setting for an IV hedonic.  

Sequence  

Stage 1  (Hedonic supply side):  
 ln Pih = α + β1 AOPENih + β2 IOPENih + β3 INDUSih + γ Xih + εih  
 where AOPEN = share of publicly accessible open space in a 500-m buffer, IOPEN = share of inaccessible open space, INDUS = share of industrial land; X = structural attributes and fine-grained location controls.  

Stage 2  (Inverse demand): combine marginal price schedule β̂ with household survey to recover Hicksian WTP; estimate how WTP varies with income and demographics using IV again to purge remaining endogeneity between chosen bundles and preferences.  

======================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variables (continuous):  

T1 = AOPENih    (share of accessible open space within 500 m)  
T2 = IOPENih    (share of inaccessible open space within 500 m)  
T3 = INDUSih    (share of industrial land within 500 m)  

Instruments  

Z1 = GBELTih  Dummy: property is *inside* the statutory green-belt/urban-containment ring (raises IOPEN, lowers developable land).  
Z2 = HIST_PARKih Dummy: pre-1932 land parcel recorded as park/common (predicts AOPEN).  
Z3 = SCHOOL_ZONEih Dummy: parcel falls inside 1980 LEA school-playing-field reservation area (predicts AOPEN).  
Z4 = PRE-1947 IND_ZONEDih Share of 1947 Development Plan lots zoned “industrial” within 500 m (predicts INDUS).  

Control observations: houses for which the instruments take value 0; i.e. properties outside the green-belt, outside historic open-space reservations, and outside historical industrial zones.  
No explicit “timing” because all variation is spatial and determined before 1984.  

======================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Instruments are strongly correlated with current land-use shares. Plausible: Reading’s post-war planning system tightly enforces historical designations.  
A2. Independence – Conditional on rich geographic fixed effects, historical designations are orthogonal to unobserved 1984 neighbourhood quality that directly affects prices. Reasonable because designations date back >30 years and pre-date current socio-economic patterns.  
A3. Exclusion – Instruments affect house prices *only* through the three land-use shares, not through other channels (e.g., school quality). We will condition on school fixed effects, distance-to-CBD, and ward-level socio-economics to buttress this.  
A4. Stable preferences / no general-equilibrium feedback within the narrow cross-section. With a single year, behavioural responses are baked into prices, but equilibrium amenities are fixed.  
A5. Linear-in-parameters hedonic functional form correctly approximates local price schedule. Will test robustness with semi-parametric (GAM) specifications.  

======================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Sorting on unobservables (e.g., high-income households choose green-belt locations for *other* amenities).  
 Mitigation: add granular coordinates (latitude×longitude polynomials), census ward fixed effects, building age dummies, and perform balance tests of observables across instrument values.  

T2.  Instruments may affect school quality or tax rates, violating exclusion.  
 Mitigation: include school catchment fixed effects and local authority tax-rate controls; run placebo IV where dependent variable is pre-determined (e.g., house age) – should be zero.  

T3.  Weak instruments for some amenities (especially AOPEN).  
 Mitigation: report first-stage F-statistics; combine instruments; if weak, use LIML / Anderson-Rubin CIs or ridge-IV.  

======================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------
library(fixest)     # fast 2SLS
library(haven)      # if Stata dta
library(readr)
library(sf)         # spatial buffers (if shapes available)
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Data -------------------------------------------------------------
house <- read_csv("reading_houses_1984.csv")      # 433 obs
hh    <- read_csv("reading_households_1984.csv")  # 206 obs

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------
house <- house |>
  mutate(
    ln_price   = log(rentalised_price),
    AOPEN      = open_access_area_500 / buffer_area_500,
    IOPEN      = open_inaccess_area_500 / buffer_area_500,
    INDUS      = industrial_area_500   / buffer_area_500,
    GBELT      = ifelse(dist_to_gb_boundary < 0, 1, 0),
    HIST_PARK  = ifelse(pre1932_park == 1, 1, 0),
    SCHOOL_ZONE= ifelse(in_school_playfield == 1, 1, 0),
    PREIND     = pre1947_industrial_share_500
  )

# 3. Main IV hedonic --------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- ln_price ~ AOPEN + IOPEN + INDUS + bedrooms + bathrooms +
                          lot_size + building_age + poly(dist_cbd,2) + ward |
                          bedrooms + bathrooms + lot_size + building_age +
                          poly(dist_cbd,2) + ward + 
                          GBELT + HIST_PARK + SCHOOL_ZONE + PREIND

hedonic_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = house, cluster = ~ward)

etable(hedonic_iv, se = "cluster")

# 4. Robustness: buffer 250 m ----------------------------------------
house <- house |>
  mutate(
    AOPEN250 = open_access_area_250 / buffer_area_250,
    IOPEN250 = open_inaccess_area_250 / buffer_area_250,
    INDUS250 = industrial_area_250   / buffer_area_250
  )

iv_formula250 <- update(iv_formula,
            . ~ . -AOPEN -IOPEN -INDUS + AOPEN250 + IOPEN250 + INDUS250 |
                 . -AOPEN -IOPEN -INDUS + AOPEN250 + IOPEN250 + INDUS250)

hedonic_iv_250 <- feols(iv_formula250, data = house, cluster = ~ward)
etable(list(Main=hedonic_iv, Buffer250=hedonic_iv_250), se="cluster")

# 5. Inverse demand (simplified) -------------------------------------
# Merge marginal prices into household data
mp <- broom::tidy(hedonic_iv) |>
        filter(term %in% c("AOPEN","IOPEN","INDUS")) |>
        select(term, estimate) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate)

hh <- hh |> mutate(
        wtp_open  = mp$AOPEN * AOPEN_hh_bundle,
        wtp_iopen = mp$IOPEN * IOPEN_hh_bundle,
        wtp_clean = mp$INDUS * INDUS_hh_bundle
      )

demand_iv <- feols(wtp_open ~ log(income) + adults + children |
                            log(income) + adults + children,
                   data = hh)
summary(demand_iv)
```

======================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory implies:

•  Accessible open space is a positive amenity ⇒ β1 > 0.  A 10-percentage-point increase in AOPEN within 500 m should raise prices by ~2–3 percent.  
•  Inaccessible open space: enters as pleasant vistas but also tightens land supply; net effect likely positive but smaller (~1 percent for 10 pp).  
•  Industrial land share strongly negative; expect β3 ≈ −0.04, i.e., an additional 10 pp of nearby industrial land lowers prices by 4 percent.  

Welfare distribution: higher-income households’ WTP elasticity should exceed that of lower-income households (income elasticity ≈ 0.5–0.6), implying benefits are skewed to richer households, while they all bear similar price-level costs from reduced housing supply – regressive net effect.  

======================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 (Relevance – strong first stage): 1  
C2 (Exclusion – no direct effect on prices): 0.5  
C3 (Independence – instruments uncorrelated with ε): 0.5  
C4 (Stable functional form / correct specification): 1  
C5 (No weak-instrument problems after tests): 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 – credible but not bullet-proof; biggest concern is exclusion, to be probed with placebo and added controls.
